etymologies.etymologyHTML:
From Middle English thinne, thünne, thenne, from Old English þynne, from Proto-West Germanic *þunnī, from Proto-Germanic *þunnuz (“thin”) – compare *þanjaną (“to stretch, spread out”) – from Proto-Indo-European *ténh₂us (“thin”), from *ten- (“to stretch”).

Cognate with German dünn, Dutch dun, West Frisian tin, Icelandic þunnur, Danish tynd, Swedish tunn, Latin tenuis, Irish tanaí, Welsh tenau, Latvian tievs, Polish cienki, Russian тонкий (tonkij), Sanskrit तनु (tanú, “thin”), Persian تنگ (tang, “narrow”). Doublet of tenuis. Also related to tenuous.

definitions.definition: Having little thickness or extent from one surface to its opposite.

quote.citation: 1853, Charles MacFarlane, Kismet: or, The doom of Turkey, page 66:
quote.text: It was no mystery at all, or a mystery covered only with the thinnest and most transparent veil, that forced abortion is a common practice among Turkish women. The horrible secret as to the means and the drugs to be employed is pretty generally known, and where ignorance prevails there are "wise women," old hags, professional abortists, who go about the country relieving matrons of their burthens for a few piastres apiece  […]

quote.citation: 1943 November – 1944 February (date written; published 1945 August 17), George Orwell [pseudonym; Eric Arthur Blair], Animal Farm […], London: Secker & Warburg, published May 1962, →OCLC:
quote.text: Out of spite, the human beings pretended not to believe that it was Snowball who had destroyed the windmill: they said that it had fallen down because the walls were too thin.

definitions.definition: Very narrow in all diameters; having a cross section that is small in all directions.

quote.citation: 2015 July 6, “Assessment of the Impact of Zoledronic Acid on Ovariectomized Osteoporosis Model Using Micro-CT Scanning”, in PLOS ONE‎[1], →DOI:
quote.text: Typically, osteoporosis causes the amount of trabecular bone to be reduced and the bone to become thinner, while the intertrabecular space enlarges and the interconnected structure of trabecular bone is disrupted.

definitions.definition: Having little body fat or flesh; slim; slender; lean; gaunt.
Of low viscosity or low specific gravity.
Scarce; not close, crowded, or numerous; not filling the space.

quote.citation: 1705, J[oseph] Addison, Remarks on Several Parts of Italy, &c. in the Years 1701, 1702, 1703, London:  […]  Jacob Tonson, […], →OCLC:
quote.text: Ferrara is very large, but extremely thin of people.

definitions.definition: (golf) Describing a poorly played golf shot where the ball is struck by the bottom part of the club head. See fat, shank, toe.
Lacking body or volume; small; feeble; not full.

quote.citation: 1690, [John] Dryden, Don Sebastian, King of Portugal: […], London:  […]  Jo. Hindmarsh, […], →OCLC, (please specify the page number):
quote.text: thin, hollow sounds, and lamentable screams

definitions.definition: Slight; small; slender; flimsy; superficial; inadequate; not sufficient for a covering.
(aviation) Of a route: relatively little used.

quote.citation: 2016, Hartmut Wolf, Peter Forsyth, David Gillen, Liberalization in Aviation, page 105:
quote.text: In short, we previously found that thin routes benefit from an increase in competition in the Spanish airline market when considering routes that were monopoly routes in 2001.

definitions.definition: Poor; scanty; without money or success.

quote.citation: 1945, Jack Henry, What Price Crime?, page 92:
quote.text: Like their friends the "draggers," the "hoisters" or shoplifters are having a thin time these days,  […]

definitions.definition: (philately) A loss or tearing of paper from the back of a stamp, although not sufficient to create a complete hole.
Any food produced or served in thin slices.

quote.citation: 1941, Theodore Roethke, “Feud”, in Open House; republished in The Collected Poems of Theodore Roethke, 1975, →ISBN, page 4:
quote.text: Exhausted fathers thinned the blood,You curse the legacy of pain;Darling of an infected brood,You feel disaster climb the vein.

The crowds thinned after the procession: there was nothing more to see.

definitions.definition: To remove some plants or parts of plants in order to improve the growth of what remains.

quote.citation: 2015 September 5, Mark Diacono, “In praise of the Asian pear”, in The Daily Telegraph (Gardening)‎[2], archived from the original on 12 September 2015, page 3:
quote.text: So floriferous are Asian pears, and the tree so laden with young fruit, that as the tree approaches maturity it is worth considering thinning the fruit (I can't quite bring myself to thin the flowers) so as to neither overburden the tree for this year nor tire it for the next. Thinning early in the season, while the fruit is small, is ideal.

definitions.definition: Not thickly or closely; in a scattered state.

quote.citation: a. 1627 (date written), Francis [Bacon], “Considerations Touching a VVarre vvith Spaine. […]”, in William Rawley, editor, Certaine Miscellany VVorks of the Right Honourable Francis Lo. Verulam, Viscount S. Alban. […], London:  […]  I. Hauiland for Humphrey Robinson, […], published 1629, →OCLC:
quote.text: Spain is a nation thin sown of people.
